newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakh reformist PM assures investors of stability.
newsitem.headline: Kazakh reformist PM assures investors of stability.

text.p: Kazakhstan's reformist Prime Minister Akezhan Kazhegeldin on Wednesday dismissed rumours of his possible resignation, sending a strong signal to foreigners eyeing investment opportunities in the resource-rich country.

"Being politicians, we are pretty serious people, and we are not going to astonish investors with our resignation... We say to investors: we are going to work consistently and for the long term," Kazhegeldin said in an interview with Reuters.

Rumours of the premier's possible resignation surfaced earlier this year after President Nursultan Nazarbayev harshly and repeatedly criticised the government for mounting social problems, which include huge wage and pension arrears.

Speculation that Nazarbayev, who has a constitutional right to form and dismiss governments, could sack Kazhegeldin's cabinet to satisfy impoverished pensioners, have worried investors lured by Kazakhstan's huge natural resources.

Foreign investors have already put over $2.0 billion into the oil industry, and total direct investment is around $3.5 billion. Kazakhstan has also raised debt internationally, and plans to borrow up to another $250 million this year.

But Kazhegeldin, 45 and a successful businessman before his appointment as prime minister in October 1994, clearly feels at home in his spacious office in an imposing government building next to Nazarbayev's newly built mansion.

"I am very grateful that investors consider me a guarantor of reforms...The privatisation process is now controlled by the government, and all the contracts are concluded on behalf of the government," he said.

In the post-communist world Kazakhstan, a former Soviet republic five times the size of France and with a population of 16.7 million, is listed among the leaders in per capita direct foreign investment.
Investors have so far put a total of around $3.5 billion into the Kazakh economy, and Kazhegeldin said he expected direct foreign investment to exceed $16 billion by the year 2000.

The premier said the government was determined to complete the privatisation of the Central Asian state's potentially multi-billion dollar oil and gas sector to strategic investors by July 1. He said the resistance of local oil barons to sell-offs to foreigners had been overcome.
"There are (company) managers who do not like privatisation at all and love this state of uncertainty...But this resistance has already been broken," he said.

Kazhegeldin said the $2.0 billion of foreign investment in the oil industry would breathe new life into the troubled sector: "This year Kazakhstan's oldest oil-rig will turn 100 and equipment is just becoming obsolete."
On Sunday Kazakhstan sold a 60-percent stake in its largest but decaying Mangistaununaigaz oil producer to Indonesia's Central Asia Petroleum Ltd for $4.35 billion.

Kazhegeldin said that stakes still remaining in state hands after sell-offs to strategic investors would be offered to portfolio investors on a stock market, which the government plans to set up by the year-end.
Investors are also likely to be offered stakes in a whole range of other promising industries.
"Kazakh aluminium, copper, zinc, ferrous metals, as well as Kazakh oil will be represented on the (equities) market -- investors must not worry," Kazhegeldin said.

He praised macroeconomic stability achieved in Kazakhstan, saying that gross domestic product was likely to grow this year by at least 1.5 percent and inflation would fall further to 17 percent. He said this was another asset to lure investors.
But Kazhegeldin conceded that his vast country, largely comprised of empty steppe, was still a mystery for many abroad.
An ancient map of Kazakhstan hanging in his room called the area "Terra Incognita", representing it as a blank white spot.
But the premier beamed with optimism: "God gave us oil and gas, and we want to be a strong energy power."
--Almaty Newsroom, +7 3272 509410
